title: The Vineyard
description: Climate, weather, soil and the grower's choices: everything that shapes a grape before it is picked.
L: What each part of the berry gives
Name the parts of a grape berry
Explain what each part gives to wine

A grape berry has skin, pulp, seeds and, around the bunch, stems. The pulp is mostly water, sugar and acid, and makes up most of the juice. The skin holds colour, tannin and most of the aroma. Seeds contain bitter, harsh tannins. Stems add tannin and a green note if they go into the fermenter.
Pulp: sugar, acid. Skin: colour, tannin, aroma.

Small berries have more skin compared with juice. Since colour, tannin and aroma sit in the skin, small-berried grapes like Cabernet Sauvignon give more concentrated wines than large-berried ones. This is also why drought years, which shrink berries, often produce deeper, more tannic reds.
Match each part of the grape to what it gives.
Most of the character of a red wine comes from the skins; most of the juice from the pulp.

Winemakers crush gently to avoid breaking the seeds, which would release bitter tannins. Some keep whole bunches, stems and all, in red fermentations for extra structure and a fresh, herbal lift. This is common for Pinot Noir and Syrah in some cellars, but only works when the stems are ripe and brown, not green.
Ripe stems can add freshness; seeds stay whole
A grape with small berries tends to give a more concentrated red wine than one with large berries.
Yes. Small berries mean more skin compared with juice, so more colour, tannin and flavour per litre.
A grape has skin, pulp, seeds and stems
Pulp gives sugar and acid; skins give colour, tannin and aroma
Small berries give more concentrated wine
Put the stages of the vine's year in order
Explain the risks at each stage

In the northern hemisphere, the vine rests in winter. Buds break in March or April. Shoots and leaves grow, then the vine flowers in late May or June. Flowers that are pollinated become berries, called fruit set. In late summer the berries soften and change colour. Harvest comes from September to October.
Budburst, flowering, fruit set, veraison, harvest

Veraison is the moment berries soften and change colour: black grapes turn from green to purple, white grapes become translucent. From then on, sugar rises fast, acidity falls, tannins and aromas mature. This takes about 6 to 8 weeks, depending on the weather and the grape.
Put the stages of the vine's year in order.
Rest in winter, then buds, flowers, berries, colour change and finally harvest.

Spring frost can kill young shoots after budburst. Cold, wet weather at flowering leads to poor fruit set, called coulure, or uneven berries, called millerandage. Hail can shred leaves and fruit. Rain near harvest can swell berries and cause rot. Each stage has its danger.
When berries soften and change colour
Veraison is the start of ripening, marked by colour change and softening. Budburst and flowering come months earlier.
The vine moves from dormancy to budburst, flowering, fruit set, veraison and harvest
Veraison marks the start of ripening, when sugar rises and acidity falls
Frost, poor fruit set, hail and rot threaten each stage
Describe cool, moderate and hot climates

Climate is the average pattern of a place over decades. Weather is what happens in a single year. Climate decides which grapes can ripen in a region; weather decides how good a particular vintage will be. Burgundy's climate suits Pinot Noir every year, but a wet, cold summer can still make a thin vintage.
Climate decides the grape; weather decides the vintage

One common measure is the average temperature of the growing season. Below about 16 degrees Celsius is cool, 16 to 18.5 is moderate, 18.5 to 21 is warm, and above that is hot. Champagne and the Mosel are cool; Bordeaux is moderate; the Barossa and much of southern Spain are warm to hot.
Which statement describes weather, not climate?
2021 was a wet, cold year in France
Bordeaux has a moderate maritime climate
A single year's conditions are weather. The other statements describe long-term patterns.

In cool and moderate regions, weather swings a lot from year to year, so vintages vary. That's why vintage charts matter in Bordeaux or Germany. In warm, dry, irrigated regions, conditions are more reliable, so vintages differ less. Wines that blend several years, like most Champagne, smooth out these differences.
Vintages vary most in marginal climates
Where are vintages likely to vary the most?
Cool and moderate regions depend on weather to ripen grapes, so years differ. Hot, irrigated regions are more consistent.
Climate is the long-term pattern; weather is a single year
Climates are cool, moderate, warm or hot by season temperature
Vintages vary most in cool and moderate regions
What the vine needs to ripen
Explain the role of heat and sunlight
Explain how water stress affects quality
Name the natural influences that cool or warm a site

The vine needs warmth to grow and to ripen sugar, tannin and aroma. Sunlight drives photosynthesis, the process that makes sugar in the leaves. Too little heat and grapes stay sour and green. Too much and sugar races ahead of flavour, while acidity drops. Balance is what growers look for.
Water: not too much, not too little

A vine needs about 500 to 700 mm of water a year. Too much and it grows leaves instead of fruit, with large, diluted berries. Mild water stress after veraison is good: berries stay small and the vine focuses on ripening. Severe drought shuts the vine down. In dry regions, drip irrigation lets growers control the dose.
Mild stress concentrates; drought stops ripening
A small amount of water stress after veraison can improve grape quality.
Yes. Mild stress keeps berries small and pushes the vine to ripen fruit instead of growing more leaves.

Large bodies of water moderate temperatures, keeping winters milder and summers cooler, like the Atlantic in Bordeaux. Cold ocean currents cool coastal regions, like the Humboldt current in Chile. Altitude cools a site by roughly 0.6 degrees per 100 m, which is why Mendoza's vineyards at 1,000 m keep their freshness. Fog does the same in Napa and Sonoma.
Water, currents, altitude and fog cool a site
Why does Mendoza make fresh wines despite its warm, sunny latitude?
Its vineyards sit at high altitude
It is close to the equator
Altitude cools the air, about 0.6 degrees per 100 m, so cool nights preserve acidity even in strong sun.
Heat ripens grapes and sunlight makes sugar
Mild water stress after veraison improves quality
Water, ocean currents, altitude and fog cool a site
Explain what soil does for the vine
Describe the effect of drainage and heat retention

Soil anchors the vine and supplies water and nutrients. The best vineyard soils are often poor, which limits vigour so the vine puts energy into fruit, not leaves. Drainage matters most: vines hate standing water, which suffocates roots and dilutes berries.

Stony and gravel soils drain fast and store heat, releasing it at night, which helps ripening in cooler areas like the Médoc. Clay soils hold water and stay cool, which suits early-ripening grapes like Merlot. Dark slate in the Mosel absorbs warmth. Chalk drains well yet stores water deep, ideal for Champagne.
Match each soil to its effect.
Each soil changes water and heat around the roots, and so the ripening.

Slopes drain well and catch more sunlight when they face the sun: south or south-east in the northern hemisphere, north in the southern. Cold air flows downhill, so slopes avoid the frost that settles in valley floors. That's why Burgundy's best vineyards lie on the middle of the slope, and the Mosel's on steep south-facing banks.
Slopes: drainage, sun and less frost
Why are slopes often better vineyard sites than valley floors?
Slopes drain, catch the sun and let cold air flow away. Valley floors usually have deeper, more fertile soils, which can lead to too much vigour.
Poor, well-drained soils focus the vine on its fruit
Gravel and slate store heat; clay stays cool and wet
Slopes give drainage, sun and protection from frost

Yield is how much fruit a vineyard produces, usually measured in hectolitres per hectare. Lower yields often mean more concentrated fruit, because the vine's energy goes into fewer grapes. Many European appellations set a legal maximum: Grand Cru Burgundy reds are capped well below basic Bourgogne. But very low yields aren't automatically better; balance is the goal.

Training is how a vine is shaped: low bush vines without wires, common in hot, dry places, or vines trained along wires, which makes the work and the sun exposure more even. The canopy is the leaves and shoots. Growers trim, position and thin leaves to give the right amount of sun and air to the bunches, preventing rot and sunburn.
Training shapes the vine; the canopy shades the fruit
Why might a grower remove some leaves around the bunches in a cool region?
To improve sun exposure and airflow
To make the vine grow faster
In a cool, damp place, more sun and air help ripening and reduce rot. In hot regions growers often keep leaves to shade the fruit.

Some growers cut off bunches in summer, called green harvesting, to lower the yield and concentrate the rest. Others prune hard in winter for the same effect. The choice depends on the grape, the vintage and what the wine is for: a fresh, everyday wine needs a different vineyard from a long-ageing one.
Cutting off some bunches in summer to concentrate the rest is called green ____.
Green harvesting removes unripe bunches so the vine ripens the remaining fruit more fully.
Lower yields often concentrate flavour, within balance
Training and canopy work control sun and air on the fruit
Green harvesting and pruning adjust the crop to the goal
Explain how growers decide when to pick
Explain why picking time shapes style

Growers measure sugar, acidity and pH, and taste the berries for flavour, seed ripeness and tannin. Pick early and the wine is fresh and lower in alcohol, but may taste green. Pick late and it is rich and riper, but can lose acidity and turn jammy. The date is one of the most important decisions of the year.
Picking date is a style decision

Hand picking is gentle and selective: pickers choose healthy bunches and can keep them whole, essential for Champagne and many fine wines. Machines shake the vine and collect berries, working fast and at night when it is cool, but they need flat, accessible vineyards and break the skins. Steep slopes like the Douro or the Mosel must be picked by hand.
Hand: selective. Machine: fast and cool.
Why are grapes for Champagne picked by hand?
Machines are banned everywhere in France
Whole bunches avoid colour and bitterness from broken skins
Champagne presses whole bunches of black and white grapes gently, so broken skins would release colour and harsh compounds. Hand picking is required there.
In hot regions, many growers harvest at night or before dawn. Cool fruit reaches the winery fresher, and less energy is spent cooling it down.
Picking grapes later in the season usually raises sugar and lowers acidity.
Yes. As grapes hang, sugar builds and acidity falls. That's why the harvest date shapes alcohol, freshness and style.
Growers measure sugar and acid and taste for ripe flavour and tannin
Hand picking is selective; machines are fast and work at night
Earlier picking means fresher wine; later picking means riper wine
Explain how the grape and the vine's year shape wine
Describe the effects of climate, soil and site
Put the vine's yearly stages in order.
Buds, flowers, berries, colour change and then the harvest.
Match each factor to its effect.
Each of these changes the temperature and so the ripening.
What does the skin of a black grape mainly give the wine?
Skins hold most of the colour, tannin and aroma; pulp holds sugar, acid and water.
Very fertile soils usually give the best quality grapes.
Not true. Fertile soils push the vine to grow leaves. Poorer, well-drained soils focus it on the fruit.
Which choices tend to increase concentration in the fruit?
Lower yields, removing bunches and mild stress all help. Heavy irrigation dilutes.
Skins give colour, tannin and aroma; small berries concentrate them
Climate sets the grape; weather sets the vintage
Soil, slope and altitude shape heat and water
Yield, canopy and picking date are the grower's key decisions
